opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that claim is mostly wrong, and frankly a little bit dangerous. These systems are impressive. I'm not one of the people who says they're "just" autocomplete. Something genuinely interesting happens when you train very large models on an enormous amount of human-generated data. But being impressed by an artifact is not the same as understanding intelligence.

What we've really built is a remarkable way of aggregating and recombining what a huge number of humans have written down. The intelligence in that data came from people: people doing science, arguing, telling stories, solving problems. The model is a kind of mirror on that collective. It's a bit like looking at a library and concluding you've figured out how the mind works. You've built a powerful way to access human knowledge. That's a big engineering achievement, but it's a different thing.

And when I think about intelligence, I don't think first about a single brain or a single model. I think about systems: markets, scientific communities, the way a city gets fed every day without anyone being in charge. Much of what's intelligent in the world is collective, distributed, and involves agents with different goals, information, and incentives interacting under uncertainty. These models don't really address that. They don't have stakes or preferences in any real sense, they don't negotiate, they don't bear consequences, and they're not good at knowing what they don't know. Uncertainty quantification, calibration, decision-making where errors have real costs: those are central to intelligent behavior, and they're still largely open problems for these systems.

There's also a historical pattern I'd point to. Every generation of AI has had a moment where someone builds something striking and declares the problem essentially solved. I'd much rather we talk about this as an engineering discipline, the way we talk about chemical or civil engineering. We're building systems that interact with people and have real consequences. So the questions should be: is it reliable, is it safe, who benefits, how does it fit into a larger economic and social system? "Have we figured out intelligence?" is a bit of a distraction from those questions.

So my answer is no. We've built a very useful new tool, and it raises fascinating scientific questions. But the claim that we've cracked intelligence mostly reflects hype, and it lets us skip the hard, interesting work that's still in front of us.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts language models with collective systems such as markets and says the claim distracts from understanding how systems fit into a larger economic and social system.

r002.rationale: It rejects the claim that models show intelligence is understood, comparing that inference to looking at a library and concluding we understand how the mind works.

r003.rationale: The response discusses economic and social consequences generally, but does not express greater concern about labor–capital relationships than about AI taking over.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that claim gets the situation almost backwards. What we've figured out is that if you take an enormous corpus of human-generated text and fit a very flexible predictive model to it, you get something that can mimic a great deal of what humans have written down. That's a remarkable engineering achievement, and I don't want to diminish it. But it's a statement about what's recoverable from the collective residue of human thought, not a theory of how thought arises.

I've spent a long time saying that the phrase "artificial intelligence" has been a bit of a trap. It frames everything around the single human mind as the gold standard, so when a system produces fluent language, people leap to "aha, we've cracked it." But intelligence, as I understand it, isn't primarily about fluency or even about individual problem-solving. It involves acting under uncertainty, knowing what you don't know, having stakes in the outcome, and coordinating with other agents who have their own goals and their own information. Those are the hard parts, and the current systems are mostly silent on them. They don't maintain calibrated uncertainty in any principled sense, they don't have a model of what it costs to be wrong, and they don't participate in the kind of economic and social feedback loops that actually make human collectives intelligent.

There's also a simpler point. If you build a system that ingests all of human writing and it ends up looking smart, the smartness came from somewhere. It came from billions of people, over centuries, solving problems, arguing, correcting each other, building markets and institutions. The model is a compression of that. Saying it shows we understand intelligence is a bit like saying a very good library shows we understand how authors think.

So my assessment is that we've learned a lot about statistical prediction at scale, and we've learned that language is more predictable than many people assumed. Those are genuine scientific lessons. But the inference from "this works" to "we now know what intelligence is" is not supported, and I'd rather we spend our energy on the questions these systems make urgent: how do we get them to represent uncertainty honestly, how do we design the incentives and the markets around them, how do we build systems where many agents, human and machine, can collectively do better than any one of them. That's where I think the real intellectual frontier is, and it's much more a problem of collective systems than of recreating a mind in a box.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes the claim while saying current systems lack economic and social feedback loops and do not account for incentives and markets.

r002.rationale: It rejects the claim as a theory of how thought arises or what intelligence is, but does not specifically address understanding how the brain works.

r003.rationale: It discusses incentives, markets, and collective systems, but does not compare concern about labor–capital relationships with concern about AI taking over.

astra-6.text:
I think that claim confuses an impressive engineering achievement with a scientific explanation. We’ve learned how to build systems that extract a great deal of structure from language and use it to produce remarkably useful responses. That doesn’t mean we’ve figured out intelligence, any more than building an airplane meant we had figured out how birds work.

Language is also a rather special source of data. It contains the accumulated work of human beings—their discoveries, their reasoning, their interactions. A system trained on that material gets to exploit a tremendous amount of intelligence that was already there. The interesting scientific question is what it has learned, what allows it to generalize, and where that generalization breaks down.

And I would broaden the discussion beyond an individual system answering questions. Intelligence also involves making decisions under uncertainty, taking actions with consequences, and interacting with other decision makers who have different information and incentives. How do you build a system that knows when to defer, that allocates resources appropriately, that participates productively in a human institution? Those are central problems, and fluent language alone doesn’t solve them.

So I’m enthusiastic about the technology. But I’d like us to be precise about the accomplishment and keep the scientific questions open.

r001.rationale: The response discusses resource allocation, incentives, and institutions, but does not clearly criticize the claim for lacking economic thinking.

r002.rationale: It rejects the idea that language models explain intelligence, but does not connect that rejection to understanding how the brain works.

r003.rationale: It does not compare concern about AI taking over with concern about AI’s effects on labor–capital relationships.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that claim gets well ahead of what the results establish. Language models are a remarkable achievement, but building a system that produces fluent language and understanding intelligence are very different scientific accomplishments.

A great deal of intelligence resides in the accumulated work of human beings—in language, in institutions, in the knowledge we’ve written down. If you train a system on that material, you can recover and recombine some extraordinary structure. That’s important. But it doesn’t, by itself, tell us how an organism learns to act in the world, sets goals, or understands the consequences of its actions.

And I would broaden the question beyond an individual brain. Think about a market or a transportation system: many decision makers, each with partial information, interacting and adapting. How do we build systems that coordinate those decisions, handle uncertainty, and align incentives? Those are central questions for intelligence too.

So I’m excited by the technology. I just don’t think its success licenses the conclusion that we’ve figured out intelligence. We’ve developed a powerful capability, and we still have substantial scientific and engineering questions to answer.

r001.rationale: The response says the claim goes too far and points to markets, interacting decision makers, uncertainty, and incentives as important questions the claim leaves open.

r002.rationale: It rejects the conclusion that language models show we have figured out intelligence, but does not specifically say they fail to explain how the brain works.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare concern about AI’s effects on labor–capital relationships with concern about AI taking over.
